title: Health Connect medical records: FHIR needs provenance as well as permission | Terra
summary: Health Connect Medical Records uses FHIR R4 and R4B. A developer guide to experimental APIs, permissions, provenance and record reconciliation.
body_markdown:
## Preserve the source before reconciling it


Health Connect groups medical records into` MedicalDataSource` objects. Google advises separate sources for unreconciled records from different systems; combining them requires reconciliation and unique resource-type and ID combinations. Resources are written through upsert operations.[Write medical data](https://developer.android.com/health-and-fitness/health-connect/medical-records/write-data) .


Keep the original source identity intact and maintain a separate reconciliation layer. If two incoming observations appear to describe the same test, retain enough evidence to explain why they were matched. Do not merge them simply because their display labels are similar.


A useful review screen should let someone move from the normalised view back to the source record. This is particularly valuable when a correction arrives or a mapping turns out to have been mistaken. You want to revise a decision, not reconstruct an entire import.


## FHIR gives the record structure


Google documents support for FHIR R4 and R4B and a defined set of resources. Observation records are categorised using their content, including codes and FHIR categories; observations outside the supported categories are not written. Google also recommends retaining the original record source in` meta.source` .[Data format documentation](https://developer.android.com/health-and-fitness/health-connect/medical-records/data-format) .


Those rules belong in the ingestion design. Track accepted, rejected, and unsupported records explicitly. A successful request should not become a cheerful assertion that the person's entire medical history is now present.


The next layer is your product's meaning. A clinical observation and a wearable-derived metric may both look like measurements, but their context can be very different. Source, collection time, units, and measurement method should travel with the value. The product can then decide which comparisons are appropriate instead of assuming that a shared label makes two records interchangeable.


## Build the small view you can explain


An initial feature could show selected clinical observations beside a wearable history, with explicit dates and links back to their sources. Keep the first version narrow enough that the team can inspect every transformation involved.


Test the unpleasant cases: duplicate-looking records, changed results, conflicting units, missing timestamps, unavailable features, and permissions withdrawn halfway through a session. A parser that accepts every happy-path sample has only demonstrated excellent manners.


For teams already collecting wearable data,[Terra's mobile SDK reference](https://docs.tryterra.co/reference/health-and-fitness-api/sdk-references/flutter) documents a Health Connect connection. It does not establish support for the experimental medical-record APIs; verify the specific resource and access path before combining that data with the wearable feed.


The payoff is a view a person can trust. They can see what the product has, where it came from, and why it appears on the timeline. They can also see what is missing.


FHIR makes exchange possible. Careful reconciliation makes a combined record understandable. We have a soft spot for that second part: the patient rarely applauds a tidy data model, but they will notice when an old result stops masquerading as a new one.
